big: Rohan puts ₹5,000 into a mutual fund SIP on the 5th of every month. This is the story of his first six months, and the number most people get wrong about it.

lines: Markets are down 15% since I started. My cousin says pause the SIP until things look better. Should I?
Good that you asked before pressing pause. First let us see what your ₹5,000 actually bought each month.

alt: Six monthly instalments buying different numbers of units as the price moves
caps: Month 1. The price is ₹100, so ₹5,000 buys 50 units.
The price slips to ₹90. The same ₹5,000 buys more units.
At ₹80 it buys the most: 62.5 units. Nobody had to be clever.
The price climbs back, so each instalment buys fewer units.
₹30,000 bought 327 units. Average cost ₹91.7, under the average price of ₹92.5.

alt: Two bars: stopping after three months versus carrying on
caps: Same fund, same prices. Rohan A stops after the dip. Rohan B carries on.
B holds nearly twice the units, because he kept buying at ₹85, ₹95 and ₹105 too.
And the units bought cheap at ₹80 are worth the same to both. Pausing only means skipping the next buys.

alt: A SIP when the price falls every month
caps: Now imagine the price never turns back.
Each instalment buys more units, but every unit is worth less.
₹30,000 became 422.8 units, worth about ₹21,141 at ₹50. A SIP lowers your average cost. It does not remove a fall.

q: Rohan's six instalments of ₹5,000 were made at NAVs of ₹100, 90, 80, 85, 95 and 105. His average cost came to about ₹91.7, below the ₹92.5 average of those NAVs. Why?
opts: The fund house gives a small discount on each instalment that you pay on time
Fixed money buys more units when the NAV is low, fewer when high
Units from an SIP are always allotted at the lowest NAV recorded in the month
The high months and the low months cancel out, leaving a lower overall figure
why: No discount exists. Every instalment is allotted at that day's NAV, so the saving cannot come from a price cut.
Fixed money divided by a low NAV gives more units, so cheap months carry more weight in the average cost.
Allotment follows the NAV of the day the money is accepted. It is never chosen as the month's lowest price.
Months do not cancel out. If they did, the cost would equal the plain average, which is ₹92.5 here.

q: After a 15% fall, Rohan's cousin says: stop the SIP now and restart when the market looks safe. What does stopping really do?
opts: It protects the units he already holds from any further fall in the market
It cancels the units he already holds at the next NAV the fund declares
It has no effect, since units from an SIP are bought at average prices anyway
It stops him buying at today's lower prices and leaves a restart date to guess
why: Units he holds still move with the NAV. Stopping the SIP only changes what he buys from now on.
Existing units stay in his folio until he redeems them. Pausing an SIP does not cancel anything.
Each instalment is bought at that day's NAV, not at an average, so skipping one means skipping a cheap buy.
Fewer instalments mean fewer units at low NAVs, and the restart date is a timing guess that SIPs exist to avoid.

q: A client's two-year SIP shows a loss. Markets are 13% lower and most of her instalments were bought at higher prices. Which reply is honest?
opts: A SIP cannot show a loss, so the statement she received must be a printing mistake
It will certainly recover within six months, so there is nothing to worry about at all
An SIP is a method, so it follows the fund: a paper loss now, with time on her side
SIPs only work in rising markets, so she should move all of it to a fixed deposit now
why: Any fund can show a loss on paper when the NAV is below the average cost. The statement is likely right.
No one can promise a recovery date. A confident promise that fails costs the client's trust.
It names the method, admits the paper loss and points to the holding period, which is the part that is true.
SIPs also buy through falls. Moving everything away after a drop turns a paper loss into a real one.

q: Rohan's SIP has run for three years. Which figure measures his return fairly?
opts: XIRR, because each instalment has been invested for a different time
The simple average of all the NAVs he bought at over the three years
Today's NAV minus the NAV of his first instalment, shown as a percentage
The expense ratio of the fund, since it shows what he earned each year
why: XIRR gives each instalment its own start date, so the return reflects how long every rupee was invested.
A plain average ignores how many units were bought at each NAV and how long each instalment has been held.
His later instalments started at other prices, so one NAV difference misses most of what he bought.
The expense ratio is a yearly cost taken from the fund. It says nothing about his own return.

pts: A SIP buys with a fixed amount, so low NAVs buy more units.
It lowers your average cost. It does not stop a fall or promise a profit.
Measure it with XIRR, and stop only when the goal changes, not when the market does.
